### Exercise 10: Render Your Document

Now render your Quarto document so that your work appears in a single report.

**(a)** Click **Render** in your `.qmd` file.

**(b)** Check that your rendered document includes:

* your answers to the interpretation questions,
* the code and output from your R exercises,
* and your recommendation for David Jones.

**(c)** If your document does not render, identify the error message and work with your group to fix it.

**(d)** What is one advantage of having your analysis and your written interpretation in the same document?

<!-- BEGIN PROFILE:r-teaching-guide -->

::: {.content-visible when-profile="r-teaching-guide"}

::: {.teaching-block}

::: {.teaching-block-header}
Teaching Note
:::

::: {.teaching-block-body}

🎯 Learning Objective

Students should:

* Render a Quarto document successfully after editing code and text
* Check that their analysis, output, and interpretation appear together in one place
* Treat rendering as a final reproducibility check rather than a formatting step
* Use error messages to begin diagnosing what went wrong when a document fails to render

✅  **Core Concepts to Highlight**

* Rendering: running the full document from top to bottom to produce an output file
* Reproducibility: if the document renders cleanly, the workflow is more likely to be coherent and repeatable
* Integrated communication: Quarto keeps code, results, and explanation together
* Error diagnosis: the goal is not to panic, but to find the first useful error message and trace it back to the relevant chunk

💬 **Suggested In-Class Prompts**

“What is Render doing now that is different from just running one line in the Console?”

“If the document renders successfully, what does that tell you about your workflow?”

“If it fails, where should you look first?”

“Why might a manager prefer one rendered report to a folder of separate files and screenshots?”

📌 **Common Misunderstandings**

* Thinking that saving the `.qmd` is the same as rendering it
* Thinking that code run in the Console will automatically appear in the report
* Ignoring the first useful error message and jumping to random fixes
* Treating rendering as ‘just presentation’ rather than a check that the analysis can run from start to finish

:::

:::

:::

<!-- BEGIN PROFILE:r-solutions -->

::: {.content-visible when-profile="r-solutions" when-profile="r-teaching-guide"}

::: {.solution-block}

::: {.solution-block-header}
Solution
:::

::: {.solution-block-body}

A successful solution is a **rendered Quarto document** that includes:

* the student’s written answers,
* the code used in the R exercises,
* the resulting output,
* and the final recommendation for David Jones.

If the document does **not** render, students should identify the first useful error message and fix the relevant issue. Common fixes include:

* removing or changing `#| eval: false` when a chunk needs to run,
* correcting a file path,
* fixing a misspelled column name,
* or correcting a syntax error in a code chunk.

A good student answer to (d) would be something like:

> Having analysis and interpretation in the same document makes the work easier to check, share, and reproduce.

:::

:::

:::
